related_questions.question: Does Congress have power over the Supreme Court?

text_blocks.snippet: Yes, Congress has some power over the Supreme Court, but it's not absolute. Congress can shape the structure and organization of the federal court system, including the Supreme Court, through legislation. They also have the power to confirm or reject presidential nominations for Supreme Court justices. Additionally, Congress can influence the Supreme Court's jurisdiction and procedures, particularly its appellate jurisdiction.
snippet_highlighted_words: Yes, Congress has some power over the Supreme Court, but it's not absolute

list.title: Establishing and Organizing Courts:
list.snippet: The Constitution grants Congress the power to create lower federal courts and determine their structure. While the Supreme Court is established by the Constitution, Congress can still shape its organization, though the specific number of justices is not explicitly dictated by the Constitution, according to the United States Courts.

list.title: Confirming Justices:
list.snippet: The Senate, part of Congress, has the sole power to confirm presidential nominations for Supreme Court justices.

list.title: Regulating Jurisdiction:
list.snippet: Congress can make "exceptions and regulations" to the Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction, meaning they can limit the types of cases the Court can hear on appeal. This power is derived from the "Exceptions Clause" in Article III of the Constitution.

list.title: Impeachment:
list.snippet: Congress can impeach and remove federal judges, including Supreme Court justices, for "high crimes and misdemeanors".

list.title: Setting Rules and Procedures:
list.snippet: Congress can establish rules of procedure for the federal courts, including the Supreme Court.

list.title: Amending the Constitution:
list.snippet: Congress can propose amendments to the Constitution, which can overturn Supreme Court decisions interpreting the Constitution.

list.title: Limitations:
list.snippet: While Congress has significant power over the courts, it cannot directly order the courts to reopen final judicial decisions or undermine the principle of judicial independence.
